The body, this physical thing God made and called good, isn't a shell to be shed but part of what God means to redeem and raise. Jesus didn't rise as a ghost. He said, "Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have," and he ate a piece of broiled fish in front of his astonished friends (Luke 24:39-43). Paul calls his resurrection "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf of a harvest. What happened to Jesus is the pattern and promise of what will happen to us. Not escape from the body. Its redemption.

Now new creation, and here N. T. Wright has spent years trying to wake the church up to what it half forgot. Look at how the Bible ends. Not with saved souls flying up to heaven, but with the opposite. John sees "the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God," and hears a voice: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:2-3). The movement is downward. Heaven comes to earth, and the two are joined. The goal of the whole story isn't humanity evacuated from a doomed creation. It's heaven and earth made one, the world we know healed and made right. As Wright likes to put it, the question isn't how we get to heaven but how heaven comes here.

Take the more spiritual hope at its strongest, because it's sincere and holds something precious. It says what finally matters is the soul's communion with God, that to be with Christ is the heart of everything. It's right about the center. Paul says, "My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better" (Philippians 1:23), and at death the believer does go to be with the Lord, a comfort the grieving must never be denied. But that isn't the final state. It's the in-between, the waiting for the day the body will rise. The Bible's last word is the trumpet, the graves opening, the dead "raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:52), and a new heaven and new earth where God "will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4). That isn't a smaller hope than souls in heaven. It's an immeasurably larger one, and more physical, which is the opposite of what we feared and far better news than we dared.

This changes how we live now, which is why it's the right place to end. If the world is going to be thrown away, nothing in it finally matters except getting souls out, and we're back in the escapism we refused last week. But if "the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption" (Romans 8:21), then everything done in the body and in the world carries a weight escapism could never give it. The cup of cold water, the work done well, the beauty made, the justice fought for, the broken thing mended, the love poured out: none of it is polishing brass on a sinking ship, because the ship isn't sinking. It's being remade.

I came to faith out of atheism, and I take seriously the suspicion that all this is a fairy tale, a story frightened people tell because they can't bear that death is the end. I won't pretend that suspicion is foolish. A hope this large could be wishful thinking, and longing doesn't prove anything. But here's where I'll leave it. The Christian hope isn't built on how badly we want death to lose. It's built on the claim that death already lost, once, in a garden outside Jerusalem, that a real man was really dead and really rose, the first piece of the new creation breaking into the old. If that happened, then the rest of it, raised bodies and a healed earth and the city coming down and the tears wiped away, isn't wishing. It's the harvest of a seed already planted.

So I won't end this study with a chart. The hope is too large to diagram, and diagramming was always partly a way of mastering what we were meant to long for. I'll end it at the edge, where the Bible ends: the dead coming out of their tombs, the world we love made right instead of thrown away, God himself come down to dwell with us, and every grave we've wept over giving back what it took. We've spent five sessions being candid about how much of the order we don't know. But we know this, and on this there's no open hand. Christ has come. Christ will come again. The dead will be raised. The world will be made right. Carry that out of this room. It's heavier than any chart, and it's the only hope big enough to live and die on.

scriptureStudy.note: "Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth ... the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God." The movement is heaven descending to a renewed earth, not souls escaping upward.
"Behold, I am making all things new." Not making all new things, but making all things new: the renewal of what already exists rather than its replacement.
"But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." His bodily resurrection is the first instance and the guarantee of ours.

"What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable ... It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." The resurrection body is real, transformed and glorified, continuous with this one yet free of death.

"The creation waits with eager longing ... that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God." Creation itself, not only souls, is to be redeemed.
Christ "will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body." The hope is plainly bodily.

The river of the water of life, the tree whose leaves "were for the healing of the nations," and "night will be no more ... for the Lord God will be their light." The Bible ends with a healed, flourishing creation and God dwelling with his people.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The recovery of the Bible's new-creation hope is in large part the recovery of a Hebrew conviction against a Greek one that slipped into the church early and never quite left. Influential strands of Greek philosophy treated matter as lower than spirit, sometimes as the soul's prison, so that salvation meant the soul's release from the body and the world. Much popular Christianity quietly absorbed this, until heaven became a bodiless elsewhere and the resurrection of the body, though confessed in the creed, was largely forgotten in favor of going to heaven when we die.

Against this, the Old and New Testaments insist that God made matter and called it good, that the body is a gift and not a prison, that the Word became flesh and rose in flesh, and that the destiny of the redeemed is not flight from creation but its renewal, with raised bodies to live in it. A group that wants to go further should notice how much the Greek picture still shapes funeral talk, hymn lyrics, and private imagination, and how much hope is lost when the resurrection is traded for a soul in the clouds. Then let the fuller hope reach back into how we treat the body, the creation, and the ordinary material life we're living now, none of which God means to throw away.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a family buries a young mother, far too soon, and at the service two kinds of comfort are offered. The first, kindly meant and common, says she's in a better place, she's an angel watching over you, her soul is free of the body at last. Part of that is true; she is with Christ, which is far better. But notice what it quietly concedes. It treats the body in the ground as the discarded part, the shell, and leaves the grave as the last word about her flesh.

The second comfort, the fuller one the Bible gives, dares to say more. The body in that ground isn't garbage. It's precious, a seed, and the God who raised Jesus bodily will raise her. This grave isn't the end of her body but its waiting place, and a morning is coming when death gives back everything it has taken. Ask the group which comfort they've heard at funerals, and which they'd want spoken over their own grave. Everyone in the room will stand at such a graveside, and the size of the hope they carry there is the point of the whole study.

leaderPrimer:
Somebody is bringing a chart. Maybe not on paper, but in their head: a full timeline with the rapture placed, the tribulation measured, the beast identified. That person has often been the most confident voice in every end-times conversation they've joined, because confidence has been the currency of this subject for a century. Your group also holds the opposite person, the one who watched a predicted date come and go, or grew up terrified of being left behind, and now goes stiff when the subject comes up.

The hazard lives between those two. Hold open hands on the timeline and the chart-bearer hears evasion, a leader too timid to say what Revelation plainly teaches. Close your hands and you've planted a flag on a second-order question and restarted a fight that has already split enough churches. The study's structure is your way through, so trust it. It sorts the last things by weight: a closed fist on what the creeds confess, that Christ will come again, the dead will be raised, and God will judge and renew all things; open hands on the sequence, the millennium and the timing of the rapture, where faithful believers have differed for centuries. Name that sorting out loud in session 1 and come back to it every week, because open hands only look like evasion when the closed fist stays hidden. Show the fist.

Give each major position its strongest voice in sessions 2 and 3, stated so well that nobody can tell where you land. If you say where you land, say it as one view among the faithful, and name the objection you can't fully answer. Expect session 5 to surprise nearly everyone, because most people assume the story ends with souls leaving for heaven, and the Bible ends with the holy city coming down (Revelation 21). Let that correction do its slow work. You aren't there to win an argument the church has never settled. You're there to help a room love Christ's appearing more than the argument, and to send people home watching instead of calculating.

faq.q: Does this study tell me which view of the end times is right?
faq.a: No, and that's deliberate, not a dodge. It presents the three major readings of the millennium, premillennial, postmillennial, and amillennial, and the dispensational rapture debate, each stated by its best advocates at full strength before any critique, because faithful, Bible-loving Christians have landed in all of them. The aim is to help you hold the question well, with open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center, not to recruit you to a camp. The study does insist on what the whole church confesses: Christ has come, he will come again to judge the living and the dead, the dead will be raised, and the world will be made right. Where the creed is firm, the study is firm. Where the creed leaves room, so does the study.

faq.q: What does it mean that the study gives each view its strongest form?
faq.a: It's the opposite of attacking a straw man. Instead of stating a view in its weakest, easiest-to-knock-down form, you state it the way its best defender would, before you offer any criticism. Every major view gets that same treatment, and none is set up to lose. So premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism each get their best scholars and strongest case from Scripture, and so does the dispensational rapture. A good test of whether you understand a view is whether you can argue for it, not just against it. This isn't a debate scored on points. It's a way of honoring people who read the same Bible and reached a different conclusion.

faq.q: Is it really okay for Christians to disagree about the end times?
faq.a: On the timeline, yes, and the church's history makes that plain. The ancient creeds don't mention the millennium or the rapture. They confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and they leave the order of events open. Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, and Calvin read the thousand years symbolically; important early voices expected an earthly reign; and serious modern scholars defend each major position. So disagreement about the shape and sequence of the end isn't a test of who belongs to Christ, and a church that makes it one draws a boundary God didn't draw. What isn't open is the center: Christ has come and is coming, the dead will be raised, and the world will be made right.

faq.q: Is the rapture in the Bible?
faq.a: A "catching up" certainly is. The word "rapture" comes from the Latin translation of 1 Thessalonians 4:17, where the dead in Christ rise and the living are "caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air." The contested question is what that describes. Dispensational premillennialism, the framework behind the Left Behind novels, developed by Darby and spread by the Scofield Bible, reads it as a removal of the church before a seven-year tribulation, and the study states that view at full strength. Historic premillennialists and amillennialists read the same passage as the church going out to welcome the returning King at his single, public coming, and they note that the two-stage structure appears clearly only in the 1800s. The study shows you both and leaves the choice open.

faq.q: If date-setting has always been wrong, why study the end times at all?
faq.a: Because the point was never to set a date. Jesus said no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son, and the disciples were told it wasn't for them to know the times the Father had fixed. Every confident prediction, from the Montanists to William Miller to the chart-makers of the last century, has been wrong, and the study takes that record as a warning. But refusing to set dates isn't the same as ignoring the Christian hope. We study the last things the way Revelation's first readers did: not to crack a code but to be steadied, to see that the slaughtered Lamb is on the throne, to long rightly for the King, and to live faithfully in the meantime. The cure for bad speculation isn't silence. It's reading well.

faq.q: What is the "already and not yet," and why does the study call it the center?
faq.a: It's the New Testament's way of describing the time we live in. God's kingdom is already here, because in Jesus it has broken into history: the King has come, the Spirit has been poured out, the decisive victory has been won at the cross and the empty tomb. And it isn't yet here in full, because the world plainly isn't made right, and we pray "your kingdom come" because it hasn't fully come. Every faithful view of the end, whatever it says about the millennium, stands on this ground. George Eldon Ladd and N. T. Wright gave it its modern shape. Living in it means working as if the kingdom matters now and waiting as people who know it's God's to finish, which guards against both fleeing the world and trying to build heaven ourselves.

faq.q: Is the Christian hope that our souls go to heaven when we die?
faq.a: That's part of it, the smaller part, and the study works to recover the larger one. It's true and comforting that at death the believer goes to be with Christ, which Paul calls "far better." But that's the in-between, not the final hope. The Bible ends not with souls floating up but with resurrection, the body raised, and new creation, the new Jerusalem coming down, God dwelling with his people on a renewed earth, every tear wiped away and death gone. N. T. Wright has pressed this on the church: the goal isn't our going up to heaven but heaven coming down. The hope is larger and more physical than the popular picture, and that's better news.

faq.q: Is the study grounded in scholarship, or is it just opinion?
faq.a: It names its sources openly so you can read further. George Eldon Ladd and N. T. Wright stand behind the "already and not yet" and the new-creation hope. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future, Kim Riddlebarger, and Sam Storms represent amillennialism. Loraine Boettner defends postmillennialism. Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock represent careful modern dispensationalism. The history is handled plainly too: the second-century chiliasts, Augustine's symbolic reading, the rise of postmillennialism in the missionary era, and the nineteenth-century origin of dispensationalism through Darby and the Scofield Bible. The study doesn't hide where ideas came from, and it doesn't use their origins as weapons, since an idea's age doesn't settle whether it's true.

faq.q: I was taught the rapture my whole life. Is this study going to tell me I was wrong?
faq.a: No. It will tell you that you were taught one serious reading among several, and ask you to understand the others before you decide. The dispensational rapture is held by millions, built by capable people, and anchored in real texts, and the study states it at full strength instead of mocking it. What it will gently question is the assumption, if you hold it, that the rapture is simply the plain reading any careful believer would reach, when the whole church, including its most literal readers, read these texts differently for eighteen centuries. You're welcome to keep your view if the text persuades you. The study only asks you to hold it as one faithful reading, not as the password to true faith, and to give those who differ the honor you'd want.

faq.q: Why does the study refuse to end with a chart or a clear timeline?
faq.a: Because the charts were part of the problem, and because the hope is too large to diagram. End-times charts give a comforting sense of mastery, of having the future pinned down and labeled, and that impulse has produced a long record of failed predictions and divided churches. The Christian hope at its fullest, the dead raised, the world made right, God come down to dwell with his people, every grave giving back what it took, isn't a sequence to be mapped but a weight to carry and a longing to feel. The last session ends deliberately at the edge of that hope, because the point was never to settle the order of events. It was to form people who hold the hope with conviction and humility, and who long for the King.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have a strong view of my own?
faq.a: Your view isn't a disqualification, but it needs care. Most leaders have a position, and that's fine. The danger is leading in a way that recruits the room, because the fastest way to break this study is for the group to work out which side the leader is on and start performing agreement to belong. So keep your own conviction quiet enough in the room that no one feels that pressure. If someone asks privately where you land, you can tell them, gently, as one reading among several, and then turn them back to the text and the other views. Your real job is to make the room state each view fairly before criticizing it, to slow down anyone rushing at a straw man, and to guard the center while keeping the timeline open.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't the idea of the world being made right just wishful thinking?
faq.a: That's a fair suspicion, and the study takes it seriously. A hope this large could be wishful thinking, and longing for the world to be made right doesn't prove it will be. But the study puts the actual Christian claim on the table, and it isn't a vague hope. It's a specific historical assertion: that one man has already risen bodily from the dead, the "firstfruits," the first instance of the renewal promised for everything else. The Christian hope isn't built on how badly we want death to lose. It's built on the claim that death already lost, once. You can examine that claim, weigh the evidence, and decide whether it holds. The study doesn't ask you to want it true. It asks you to consider whether it is.

timeline.event: Under the persecution of Antiochus IV, Daniel's visions of beasts and kingdoms, and of a God who outlasts every empire, give God's people the language Revelation later draws on. (Many scholars date the book's final form to this crisis; others date it much earlier.)
Jesus announces that the kingdom of God is in the midst of his hearers and also teaches them to pray for it to come, and he declines to name the day or hour of the end.

Paul writes to the Thessalonians to comfort those grieving believers who have died, describing the dead in Christ rising and the living caught up to meet the Lord, the passage behind the later idea of the rapture.

John writes Revelation to seven churches in Asia Minor under Roman pressure, to steady them with the vision that the slaughtered Lamb reigns and Rome doesn't. (Some scholars date it earlier, in the 60s.)
Papias, Justin Martyr, and Irenaeus look for a literal earthly reign of Christ, an early premillennial hope often called chiliasm, though it is never the only view in the early church.
Montanus and his followers in Phrygia expect the New Jerusalem to come down there, an early instance of fervent expectation that didn't come to pass.

Augustine writes The City of God, whose twentieth book reads the thousand years as the present age of the church. This symbolic reading shapes Western Christianity, Catholic and later Protestant, for more than a thousand years.
The Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them, keep the broadly Augustinian symbolic reading of the millennium.

Postmillennial hope flowers in the era of revival and expanding missions, as confidence in the gospel's power to transform the world makes a coming age of righteousness feel near to many serious believers.
John Nelson Darby, among the early Plymouth Brethren in Britain and Ireland, develops dispensationalism, with its sharp distinction between Israel and the church and its pretribulation rapture.
William Miller's followers, having fixed the return of Christ for October 22, wait, and the day passes into what they called the Great Disappointment.
The Scofield Reference Bible is published, printing Darby's framework in notes beside the biblical text and spreading it across American Christianity.

George Eldon Ladd's books, from Crucial Questions about the Kingdom of God (1952) to The Presence of the Future (1974), bring the "already and not yet" into evangelical scholarship alongside a historic premillennialism without a two-stage coming.
Anthony Hoekema publishes The Bible and the Future, a careful modern statement of amillennialism and the new-creation hope.
N. T. Wright publishes Surprised by Hope, pressing on the church that the Christian hope is resurrection and the renewal of all creation, heaven coming down to a healed earth.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. People usually either avoid this subject or fight about it, and you came to do neither. Before we start, three things. First, this study has one rule above the others: open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center. We'll disagree freely about the order and shape of the end, because faithful Christians have for centuries, and we won't disagree about what the whole church confesses, that Christ has come, he will come again, the dead will be raised, and the world will be made right. Second, we'll state every view at its strongest before anyone argues against it. If you find yourself wanting to knock a view down, first state it so well that someone who holds it would nod. Third, none of us is above this, me included. We've all felt the pull of date-math in the dark and of treating the end as an escape from a world we're meant to love. Tonight we're looking at this: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says a word. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only true ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've stated the views fairly and held them at their strongest. Now let's bring it home, off the chart and into the way we actually live and hope and treat the people across the table from us, because that's where this matters or doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop here, and notice we're stopping without a tidy chart, on purpose, because the point was never to pin down the order of events. Take the center out of this room with you this week, that Christ has come and is coming and will make the world right, and hold it more tightly than any timeline. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if you came in sure your view was the only faithful one, carry out a little more room for the brother and sister who read it differently, because that charity is part of the hope too. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the humility it took to be in this room.

plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the one rule, open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center, and agree to state every view at its strongest before any content.

Week 3: Session 2, part one, premillennialism and postmillennialism, each at full strength.
Week 4: Session 2, part two, amillennialism at full strength, then the posture of holding all three with open hands.
Week 5: Session 3, Rapture, Tribulation, and the Dispensational Debate, the dispensational case at full strength.
Week 6: Session 3 continued, the historic-premillennial and amillennial alternatives, and what is and isn't at stake.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: A central modern recovery of the new-creation hope, that the goal isn't souls going up to heaven but heaven coming down to a renewed earth. The backbone of session 5.

bibliography.title: The Presence of the Future, and A Theology of the New Testament
bibliography.author: George Eldon Ladd
bibliography.note: The classic evangelical statement of the "already and not yet" and of a careful historic premillennialism distinct from dispensationalism. Supports sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Bible and the Future
bibliography.author: Anthony A. Hoekema
bibliography.note: A careful and influential statement of amillennialism and the new-creation hope. Essential for hearing amillennialism at full strength in session 2.

bibliography.title: A Case for Amillennialism: Understanding the End Times
bibliography.author: Kim Riddlebarger
bibliography.note: A clear, accessible modern defense of amillennialism. Supports session 2.

bibliography.title: Kingdom Come: The Amillennial Alternative
bibliography.author: Sam Storms
bibliography.note: A detailed contemporary case for amillennialism, to be presented fairly alongside the other views in session 2.

bibliography.title: The Millennium
bibliography.author: Loraine Boettner
bibliography.note: A vigorous defense of postmillennialism and the confidence that the gospel will transform the world before Christ returns. The best voice for the postmillennial view in session 2.

bibliography.title: Progressive Dispensationalism
bibliography.author: Craig A. Blaising and Darrell L. Bock
bibliography.note: A careful modern refinement of dispensational premillennialism, useful for stating the dispensational case at full strength rather than in caricature. Essential for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views
bibliography.author: Robert G. Clouse, editor
bibliography.note: A classic volume in which advocates of each major view state and defend their own position. Ideal for sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: Four Views on the Book of Revelation
bibliography.author: C. Marvin Pate, editor
bibliography.note: Sets the major approaches to reading Revelation side by side. Helpful for session 1 on genre and for seeing why the same text yields different schemes.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The source of the symbolic reading of the thousand years as the present church age (Book 20), which shaped Western Christianity for over a thousand years. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: The Last Things: An Eschatology for Laymen
bibliography.author: George Eldon Ladd
bibliography.note: A short, accessible treatment of the Christian hope. Supports sessions 4 and 5.

bibliography.title: Reversed Thunder: The Revelation of John and the Praying Imagination
bibliography.author: Eugene H. Peterson
bibliography.note: A pastoral reading of Revelation as worship and formation rather than prediction. A good companion to session 1.

furtherReading: Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for readers who want to sit longer with the new-creation hope and the recovery of resurrection behind session 5.
The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views, Robert G. Clouse, editor, for anyone who wants to hear advocates of each major view defend their own position.
The Bible and the Future, Anthony Hoekema, for the fullest careful statement of amillennialism and the symbolic reading of the thousand years.
Progressive Dispensationalism, Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock, for the dispensational view in its most careful modern form rather than through the popular novels.
Reversed Thunder, Eugene Peterson, for reading Revelation as worship and formation rather than a code to crack.

glossary.definition: The study of the last things, how the story ends, including death, resurrection, judgment, Christ's return, and the new creation. The study holds its contested parts with open hands and its central confession with a closed fist.

A kind of writing, including Daniel and Revelation, born among God's persecuted people, dense with symbol, number, beast, and vision, written to steady the faithful with the assurance that God reigns and the oppressor will fall. Not a coded calendar.

Latin for a thousand years, the period mentioned in Revelation 20, read by the church three ways: a future earthly reign after Christ returns, a long age of righteousness before he returns, or the present church age understood symbolically.

The reading that Christ returns before ("pre") a thousand-year reign on earth, taking Revelation 19 and 20 as consecutive. Held in a historic form by George Eldon Ladd and in a dispensational form by Darby and his heirs.

The reading that the gospel will so advance through history that the world enters a long age of righteousness, after ("post") which Christ returns. It draws on the parables of leaven and mustard seed and the promise that the knowledge of the Lord will fill the earth. Defended by Loraine Boettner.

The reading that the thousand years is symbolic, the present age between Christ's two comings, in which he reigns from heaven and Satan is bound from deceiving the nations. Held by Augustine and the Reformers, and defended today by Hoekema, Riddlebarger, and Storms.

A system developed by John Nelson Darby in the 1800s and spread by the Scofield Bible, dividing history into distinct ages and keeping a sharp distinction between Israel and the church, from which its pretribulation rapture follows.

From the Latin for the "catching up" Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 4, the gathering of believers to meet the returning Lord. Whether it is a separate event before a tribulation or the church welcoming Christ at his single, public coming is contested among faithful readers.

A time of intense trouble before the end. Dispensationalism reads a specific future seven-year tribulation from which the church is removed; other views read tribulation language as the pressure the church lives under throughout this age.
The New Testament's description of the present time, in which God's kingdom has already broken in through Christ but hasn't yet fully come. The shared center of every faithful view of the end.

The conviction that God's kingdom has truly begun in Jesus, launched at the cross and resurrection, while it awaits completion at his return. The "already and not yet" named from the side of the "already."

The Bible's final hope, the renewal rather than destruction of the world, a new heaven and new earth joined when the city of God comes down, God dwelling with his people, every tear wiped away and death gone.
The creedal hope that the dead will be raised bodily, not only that souls survive death, patterned on Jesus' bodily resurrection as the firstfruits.
The condition of believers between death and resurrection, consciously with Christ, which Paul calls "far better." Real and comforting, but not the final hope.

quoteCards: Read the end rightly and it doesn't feed your speculation. It steadies your faith.
Every confident date has been wrong. That record isn't a footnote. It's a warning.
Open hands on the timeline. A closed fist on the center.
You understand a view when you can argue for it, not just against it.
The escapist and the date-setter look like opposites. Both refuse the meantime.
The goal isn't our going up to heaven. It's heaven coming down to a world made right.
